I note that I provoke an automatic reflex in the hon. member for Halifax whenever I rise. I want to assure him that this is a matter which is of great concern to more than just the people in one particular province.
You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that last evening, under the administrative item I had some remarks to make with respect to the advertising approach used by the ethical drug industry in advertising its products to the medical profession. I should like to make one other reference to this matter before I make inquiry of the minister. I should like to point out that the drug manufacturers in many cases, or at least in one case of which I have knowledge, make use of so-called invisible physicians to prove the efficacy of their particular product. I should like to make reference to an article which appeared in the January 3, 1959 edition of Saturday Review, at pages 38, 39 and 40 of that particular edition. This has reference to an advertisement or a brochure produced by the Pfizer Laboratories, which is a division of Charles Pfizer and Company, a drug manufacturer in the United States, and has reference to a drug called sigmamycin. There is here on this particular page a reproduction of part of that particular advertisement. It is headed as follows:
Everyday .. . Everywhere . .. More and more physicians find sigmamycin the antibiotic therapy of choice.
Then it lists the names, addresses and telephone numbers of a number of specialists

who had made use of this particular drug and had endorsed it. The cards of four of them are reproduced here and reference to another four is made in name only. The four whose cards are reproduced are as follows:
Thomas Wright, M.D.
Eye, ear, nose and throat
And an address and phone number are given in Lowell, Massachusetts.
E. N. Stephens, M.D.,
Pediatrics
And a phone number, address and office hours are given. The address is Taylor street, Portland, Oregon.
Joseph Burns, M.D., internal medicine, 245 South 1st street, Miami, Fla.; Paul D. Friend, M.D., dermatology, 1345 Eastbourne avenue, Tucson, Arizona;
As I said before, there are others; a urologist, a general practitioner, a surgeon, just picking them out of the article. The article goes on:
The staff of SR/Research has tried to reach each of the eight individuals named. Telephone calls have been made, telegrams have been sent, and the following letter has been written;
"Dear Dr.-:
If you have published any of your clinical experiences with sigmamycin, I would appreciate your sending me the reference or preferably a reprint, if available.
Then reading further:
The telephone operators have reported all of the phone numbers to be false numbers, Western Union has reported inability to find such persons, and seven of the eight letters had been returned unclaimed by the post office-
Four of those letters are reproduced in photostat form which were returned unclaimed with various postal marks on them to indicate they were returned by the post office because the doctors to whom they were addressed could not be found. In fact they did not exist. Here is one indication only as shown by this particular article where Pfizer and Company, I say, attempt to mislead other doctors by indicating that some members of the medical profession, specialists, general practitioners and surgeons alike, had used and had endorsed it, had found that this particular drug was a good drug for the purpose for which it was to be used.
I also read other references yesterday from a paper by Professor Nickerson, professor of pharmacology and therapeutics at Manitoba university, which paper was co-authored by an associate professor of medicine whose name I have forgotten at this moment. The gist of Professor Nickerson's article was that perhaps we should have some form of control by a public authority such as the food and drug directorate over the type of advertising material that is prepared by these drug

manufacturers and which is sent out to various medical doctors' offices across the country.
It is quite true that the reference I have just made to the Saturday Review concerns the United States and only makes mention of the names of each of the doctors who are supposed to have existed but in fact who did not exist. But it is also a fact Charles Pfizer and Company has a subsidiary which sells various pharmaceuticals in Canada.
I wonder if the minister would indicate what has been the experience of the food and drug directorate so far as checking the advertising material which drug manufacturers produce in the ethical trade compared with the type of checking and editing that is made of such food and drug advertisements directed to the consumer such as in the proprietary medicine field?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF GENERAL HEALTH GRANTS FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1960-61
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the food and drug directorate do check on the advertising of patent medicines and preparations which are on the shelf or are sent through the mail or even sold on the streets, as well as advertisements concerning goods which may be ordered by mail, and that sort of thing. But we are not in a position due to staff shortage to concern ourselves particularly with the advertisements going to doctors. We feel they are possibly sufficiently knowledgeable to be aware of the situation. We are concerned with it but we just do not have the staff to do this at the time and we feel that our responsibility is to the public rather than to the medical profession.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF GENERAL HEALTH GRANTS FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1960-61
speechtext:
May I just follow that up. I believe this is probably the reason why there were no checks by public authorities of the correctness or otherwise of brochures and advertising material for the ethical drugs which were directed to doctors, because doctors themselves are sufficiently trained and knowledgeable with regard to the intricacies of the field of medicine and would be able to determine whether any advertisement was incorrect or otherwise. Therefore they could disregard the advertisements which were not correct and only use those drugs which had been clinically tested and proved to be safe.
Of course I am not casting any reflection whatsoever on the medical profession. However, I have spoken with four or five medical men in the city of Ottawa and with one who is a member of this house and they all say that they are virtually swamped with advertising material. I have heard estimates ranging from 300 pieces of literature a year
Supply-Health and Welfare to perhaps a thousand pieces a year which get into a doctor's office advertising particular medicines and things like that.
All the doctors I have spoken to in this city say that most of it is wasted. They are very selective and naturally will pick out that piece of advertising material relating to pharmaceuticals which they would use in the normal course of their practice and they discard that advertising material they would not normally use or which is new material about which they would rather have additional tests made to prove its efficacy. They all say there is far too much of it. It is far too sketchy and it is designed solely to leave the brand name of the product in the mind of the doctor. The initial advertising material makes very sketchy reference to the clinical tests given to a particular drug, and if the doctor is interested he can follow it up by consulting the detail man as he comes around or he can get the information himself.
I read into the record yesterday the results of a casual survey which had been conducted. The article I read did not give any indication as to exactly where this particular survey had been conducted, amongst how many doctors it had been conducted, or who had conducted it; but Professor Nickerson pointed out that the majority of the physicians who were contacted who were utilizing a new and effectively advertised analgesic did not know that it was simply the standard A.P.C., which is listed as acetyl-salicylic acid, in other words a well-known headache cure. Professor Nickerson pointed out that this had been advertised by the ethical drug industry as a new and effective analgesic, yet in fact it was something which had been on the market for many years, plus a little barbiturate.
The article pointed out that certain physicians did not know the composition of pharmaceuticals of certain types and that they ordered by a simple number of like designation. As a result, it continues, two patients died of intoxication because of the use of these preparations. One or two further references are made to similar incidents.
As I say, I have heard reference to the effect that this is an attempt to brainwash doctors. I have no remarks to make which are derogatory in any way of doctors themselves. I have the greatest admiration for the persons in the medical profession whom I have met. They have been people of extremely high calibre, solely concerned with the health and welfare of their patients. But I point out that some of the advertising which is directed toward these doctors is absolutely untrue, false and misleading, and I express the view very strongly that there should be some check against it.

Supply-Health and Welfare
If the ethical drug industry itself intends to persist in this sort of practice about which I read from the Saturday Review a while ago in which they pull out of thin air a list of eight doctors and state that these eight doctors have used a particular pharmaceutical and found it good, whereas in fact the eight doctors do not exist, it is obviously time that this false and misleading type of advertisement should not be allowed to continue. If the ethical drug industry-and, again,
I cannot understand how the word "ethical" got into it-is going to carry on this false and misleading advertising and if it is not prepared to put its own house in order, then some public authority will have to do it in order to ensure that in the final analysis the consumer is protected to the fullest possible extent and also that the doctor himself is protected against having his office invaded by false propaganda which misleadingly states a product to be something which it is not.
I know that the food and drug directorate may be overworked at the moment, but I do think steps should be taken at some time to ensure that the public of Canada are not left at the mercy of these misleading claims such as are made by Charles Pfizer and Company, not for the purpose of producing more effective drugs but for the purpose of racking up tremendous profits. There has to be some protection placed between such firms and the public.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF GENERAL HEALTH GRANTS FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1960-61
speechtext:
We are talking about the ethical drug industry, and this is an industry wihch produces drugs which are only sold on prescription. The great majority of the advertising of this industry is not directed to the consuming public; it is directed to the doctors, and I still say that outlets such as Charles Pfizer and Company about which I read from the Saturday Review-and I take the report to be correct, because I do not know of any libel action instigated by Pfizer against the Saturday Review-should be prevented from carrying on advertising of this type. speechtext:
On June 13 I directed a question to the minister on the orders of the day as to the possibility of lipstick colouring containing cancer-causing agents. The minister at that time replied in part that as far as the colouring now being put in lipstick was concerned there was no evidence that amounts normally absorbed into the system could create any risk to health.
Since that time I have read in a Washington dispatch that the food and drug administration in the United States was continuing to study this question because it suspected these cancer-causing agents, and on June 16 in Washington, according to a dispatch from that city, a decision to ban the use of 14 coal tar colours in lipsticks was announced by the United States government. Coal tar colours had been mentioned by the officials as a possible cause of certain types of cancer.
I suppose as a result of my question, which I asked on account of correspondence which I had received, there has been a greater interest aroused, and I have received further correspondence. I want to make it clear that I have no personal concern in this matter, because I am far beyond the age to indulge in osculatory exercises; I am doing this because persons have written to me and shown concern, not only about the colouring used in lipstick but also in respect to cosmetics imported from the United States such as hair dyes and nail polish which may or may not contain harmful ingredients which could produce toxic conditions in the human body over a period of time if used constantly.
My question to the minister is this: would he inform the committee what the division is doing to check on these substances which apparently are causing the food and drug division of the United States government some concern in order to make certain that the health of the Canadian people and, in this case, particularly of the ladies in whom I am sure we are all interested or at any rate maybe some of the younger hon. members are, is protected.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF GENERAL HEALTH GRANTS FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1960-61
speechtext: We are, of course, continuing to study this matter. Our regulations regarding colouring agents are very tight and very severely administered. As a consequence we are not worried about cosmetics in Canada. However, we are following the developments in the United States very closely.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF GENERAL HEALTH GRANTS FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1960-61
speechtext: That was the question I was about to ask. Thank you.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF GENERAL HEALTH GRANTS FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1960-61
speechtext:
The annual report of the department with regard to narcotic control and the authority of the minister and the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act reminds us that there has been no marked trend either way in the number of addicts in Canada over the last five years. The last figure given is for 1958-I refer to page 94 of the department's annual report-and the number of drug addicts given for 1958 is 3,412, a slight increase over 1957 and a somewhat larger increase over 1956 but a reduction compared with 1955 and an increase of about 200 over 1954. This figure, however, represents much economic loss and much human suffering. In this country we must try to deal with this problem through the Criminal Code, through the operations of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act and through the health departments of the provinces. I rise at this time mainly to request the minister to comment on the problem as he sees it at the present time.
I note that there were 522 convictions registered under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act during the calendar year and that this represented 494 persons of whom 336 were male and 158 female. We are all aware of the great misfortune that attends those who are addicted to this practice but we in this country and in other countries have not yet succeeded in finding a formula that really meets the problem.
I have before me a report which appeared in the New York Times in the month of March in which the commissioner for drug control in the United States pointed out that in his judgment the heavier mandatory jail sentences for agents has resulted in a decline in narcotic usage and in what is called dope peddling in that country. It will be remembered that pursuant to the recommendations of a committee of the other house four years ago there was an increase provided in the terms of punishment which could be meted out by the courts in respect of those found guilty of a violation of the act. It would be interesting to know whether the minister subscribes to the view of the United States commissioner that as a result of the increase in the severity of jail sentences that are now open to those exercising judicial administration of this act there has been any decline in the usage of drugs or in the activities of peddlers in the manner suggested by the United States commissioner.
On several occasions during the past six months the Minister of Justice has made public declarations about his intentions in regard to this matter. The Minister of National Health and Welfare will recall the question 79951-0-336
Supply-Health and Welfare I put to him this session-I believe in the month of February-when I asked whether he regarded this matter as one that came within the responsibility of the Minister of Justice or as one coming within his own competence. I am not clear in my own mind at the moment what the reply was. I think it was to the effect that the Minister of Justice has some responsibility under the Criminal Code but that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has a responsibility on the health side.
If that was the reply, of course, that is a clear statement of the demarcation of the functions that exist as between the two ministers. It has always been the practice for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to regard this as his matter because in many respects, perhaps in so far as the majority of drug addicts are concerned, the problem has deep health aspects in addition to criminal aspects. Be that as it may I have no quarrel with the two ministers. What I am more concerned about, as we all are including the ministers themselves, is that as satisfactory a solution as we can find be provided for this problem.
The Minister of Justice said in British Columbia and also in Winnipeg, I believe, that he hoped within the foreseeable future to carry on some discussions with the provincial governments for the purpose of dealing more effectively with this matter of narcotic control. The hon. gentleman did not say whether that had to do with further punitive measures. From what the hon. gentleman said in this chamber in answer to my question it was not clear exactly what he had in mind. I asked him whether or not it was the intention of the federal government, for instance, to make available in British Columbia quarters where there could be provided treatment for drug addicts on the assumption that this is basically a health problem. I did not receive a satisfactory reply to this question. It may be that the Minister of Justice was thinking of the experience in the United States, particularly in Lexington, Kentucky, where they combine both the principle and method of treatment with confinement, where there is an admixture of the criminal and the patient, with results that I do not think have yet been properly and finally assessed. I would be interested in knowing from the Minister of National Health and Welfare if that is what the Minister of Justice had in mind. Obviously there must have been consultations between the two ministers in this regard.
Is there any intention of which the minister is aware-and this would be within
5328	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare his ministerial interest and concern even though it might be more strictly applicable to the Minister of Justice-to give consideration to the imposition of punishments heavier than those now provided for under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act and under the Criminal Code? Is there any contemplation such as is frequently suggested that the sentence which ought to be meted out is a sentence which must go away beyond even confinement? It has been suggested that there is no more effective punishment for certain crimes having to do with drug traffic than capital punishment. I am not advocating that and I would think that would not be the most constructive way of dealing with the problem but that is a suggestion that has been made in this house once this session.
I do not know what the government has in mind. Is the government thinking merely of attempting to do what has been done in Lexington, Kentucky, or was the Minister of Justice just out on a fishing expedition? Was this really a serious effort on the hon. gentleman's part and, if it was, would the minister whose estimates we are considering give us the details?

We have a responsibility for the supervision of the legitimate distribution of narcotic drugs. The whole matter is continually being studied by my department and the Department of Justice.

He is the hon. gentleman who recommends to the Department of Justice the personnel employed in prosecutions. He is the one who provides for the compensation paid to prosecutors. The minister surely cannot say, because the Minister of Justice may have some pet scheme


about which he is unaware, that this is a matter concerning which information cannot be supplied to the committee. I would remind him that that has not been the attitude of his predecessors. I am not talking about myself because I would be a very poor example for the minister and I am not suggesting that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF GENERAL HEALTH GRANTS FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1960-61
speechtext: Thank you very much.

maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF GENERAL HEALTH GRANTS FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1960-61
speechtext: The other ministers never hesitated to indicate this.

speechtext: If the minister's reply is along that line it is a reply he should have made a while ago. He is now saying that government policy will be announced in due course. maintopic: DISTRIBUTION OF GENERAL HEALTH GRANTS FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 1960-61
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very interested in this item. I notice that we are contributing a considerable amount of money to various health and welfare organizations in Canada. I should like to refer specifically tonight to the donation of $35,000 to the Canadian welfare council. I quite realize that they are doing wonderful work but at this time I should like to refer to part of the report of the president of the council for 1958. I wish to read part of the report to substantiate my argument.
Because of the nature of our membership, we act from time to time as spokesman for welfare interests in Canada, and it seems to me that the council has for this reason a particular and effective place in Canadian life. Two recent activities illustrate this function. Last year when we had a large influx of refugees from Europe, the council acted both as a spokesman and a co-ordinator in resolving many of the problems which arose. Then the council's discussions of certain social security issues stimulated our members' interest and drew outstanding participants from a wide field.
There are two sides to this role of spokesman. One is that the community at large or legislative bodies look to the council for advice, counsel and suggestions. The other is that any or all groups and individuals with an interest in social welfare find in the council a forum for the expression of their views, and frequently discussion leads to an influential public statement on social welfare policy.
But of course national planning and action is only one side of our activities. In this report, which gives examples of our work in all its branches, we can look beyond the reports, surveys, conferences and briefs to governments. We can see a homeless child placed in a new home by an agency the council has helped to improve its practices; old people benefiting from a program set up with council advice; an unemployed man regaining his self-respect through financial assistance and services the council has worked to bring about; an ex-convict going straight because of help the council has promoted.
I have only read part of the report of the president of the Canadian welfare council for 1958. Within the last couple of days a case has been brought to my attention

Supply-Health and Welfare which is actually not a welfare case but I wish to bring it up at this time. A young lad with his wife and three very small children got off the train in Ottawa the day before yesterday and we were very fortunate in being able to take care of them for one night. In the meantime we got in touch with various people for advice and assistance without receiving any help at all. We got in touch with practically all the social service agencies in Ottawa, the traveller's aid, the public welfare society, neighbourhood services, city services, social services, the Salvation Army and last of all a member of the Department of National Health and Welfare, in order to try to solve the problem.
As I look at the picture now, no one has been able to do anything for a Canadian citizen who has served in the armed services overseas. This is an emergency that should be met now, not tomorrow, not next week, not next month. It was necessary that something be done today and it was impossible for us to find anybody in the city of Ottawa or the government department who could deal with this case on an emergency basis.
If leadership is being given by the Canadian welfare council to local organizations such as I have mentioned, then something is definitely lacking because the incident I have described should not have taken place under any circumstances. I have looked through this report and I find that immediate assistance can be given to indigent travellers, to refugees and to immigrants coming into the country. It can be given to prisoners who are out on parole and it can also be given to offenders released from our penitentiaries.
But no assistance or help, and I am speaking now of immediate help, can be given to a Canadian citizen who comes to the city of Ottawa or any other Canadian city. He is not able to get any immediate help to look after his wife and his children until certain applications have been made, investigations have been carried out and all the red tape has been gone through. I am simply using this case as an example and I am not reflecting on some of the good work this organization does accomplish. Nevertheless, I think some action should be taken to look after cases which require immediate attention.
After spending two days on this problem there is, as far as I can see, no welfare service that is capable of or able to handle problems on an emergency basis without going through a tremendous amount of formality. I am bringing this matter to the attention of the committee. I hope that some good will come out of my having done so and that the minister will find time to look into the matter through the welfare department.

If it is possible for us, as it is and as I think it should be, to provide assistance to the needy not only in our own country but in other countries such as assistance for refugees, it would be difficult to argue that we should not provide assistance to our own people. Under the public assistance act it would be possible to provide assistance in the case mentioned by my hon. friend if the province to which the individual had come had an agreement with the province from which he came providing for a reciprocal arrangement. It is surprising to me that it was not possible for the hon. member to get some indication from the various sources he mentioned as to how help might be provided. Because of the particular experience he had with regard to this case I do not think he would want to imply that the national welfare council is not a body that should not receive the support of parliament. The Canadian national welfare council was strongly supported this afternoon by the hon. member for Kootenay West who at one time, I believe, was one of its national executives and may still be. In any event, he was.
This is a body of public-spirited citizens who do not provide relief administration but who are mainly concerned with promoting an interest in and an understanding of social welfare problems and social security programs. The minister will recall that yesterday I referred to a submission which had been made to the government of Canada in 1958, in 1959 and again this year by the Canadian national welfare council. That body had pointed out that commendable as was the social security program there were existing gaps, there was a pattern yet to be fully formulated and that as a means of accurately defining activities in social security by the two senior levels of government and also for the purpose of making an assessment of the

flexibility of the existing programs, a royal commission should be appointed by the government. This point was also emphasized by the hon. member for Kootenay West but the minister has not given us a reply as to whether the government proposes to accept the suggestion made by the national welfare council.
Supplementary questions were asked on this subject during the present session, and I find that the point of view of the national welfare council was referred to by implication recently in an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal. That article posed the question: "Are Canada's social security laws being abused?" We recall that there have been references this session to the alleged abuse of certain social welfare measures in this country. I think that some of these abuses have possibly been overemphasized and, again, others may not have been recognized, but I think the minister should indicate to the committee what consideration he has given to this recommendation of the national welfare council.

Supply-Health and Welfare would have assisted him at least on a temporary basis until he could be settled.
I suggest this situation adds weight to the argument made by the hon. member for Essex East and later by the hon. member for Kootenay West that there are gaps in our national welfare system which have to be filled, and I trust the minister will have a few words to say with regard to the unfortunate case which has been brought to his attention.

First, I cannot express myself too strongly about the particular situation which arose on that occasion, and if the hon. member for Kootenay East will bring this question to my notice personally I shall be happy to examine it and see what might be done in the future to prevent a similar situation from arising. I should like to think that such an unfortunate situation would never have to arise in this Canada of ours. However, I do not suppose we shall ever be perfect. We have made a great deal of headway during the last few years, I think there can be no doubt about that, and I trust that as time goes on all these gaps will eventually be closed.
The hon. member for Essex East brought in another angle concerning the Canadian welfare council, suggesting that I did not reply to a question directed to me asking whether the government had considered the proposals made to us by that body. The government appointed Lieutenant General Graham, former chief of staff, to make on behalf of the government of Canada a survey of all aspects of Canada's civil defence. We did ask the government to give us this report, but he regarded it as confidential. Although it had been discussed with the provinces it was felt that the government was not disposed to give its recommendations to parliament. I regret that because it would give us an opportunity, apart from security matters, to make an assessment of the recommendations of General Graham.
The Prime Minister said on March 23, 1959 that the government had decided to make rearrangements in the division of responsibility for civil defence. As I understand it, the health and welfare aspects of civil defence continue to be the responsibility of the hon. gentleman and his department. The emergency measures organization is to be attached to the privy council and it is to co-ordinate the work of other agencies in the field of civil defence planning and the like. The Department of National Defence is to be entrusted with the responsibility of warning of an attack, the location and the

Supply-Health and Welfare monitoring of explosions and radioactive fallout, the assessment of damaged areas, contamination and clearing of such areas and the rescue of the injured.
It seems to us that the minister ought to explain the situation as he has done so only in part in the committee. We ought now to be given this information because of the importance of the matter if for no other purpose than emphasizing to the public what the chain of authority is.
The minister is in charge of health and welfare measures. The office of the privy council is in charge of the work of coordination. The army is in charge of those functions which I have just outlined. The Prime Minister told us that the Minister of National Defence is the minister to whom one must look for ministerial direction in the first instance. Since in the national health and welfare report reference is made to the emergency measures organization one, I think, must ask the minister which minister, the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or the Minister of Justice, which of those four, is responsible for the decision that must be taken in the event of an emergency. Is it a decision that must be made by the Prime Minister? What active interest does the Prime Minister have in the particular responsibility which comes under the privy council? Is this matter left to the Minister of National Defence? If an attack were to take place tomorrow and a very important decision had to be made which one of the four ministers would make the decision?
The Prime Minister said that the question was one that should be addressed to the Minister of National Defence. The Minister of National Defence says it is one that should be addressed to the Prime Minister. This matter ought to be resolved so that we shall have a clear idea as to where-in the event that what we all hope sincerely will never happen, does happen-the ultimate authority and responsibility lie. I am asking the minister now on these estimates to outline the facts for us.
I should also like to know from the minister when the last meeting of the federal-provincial advisory committee was held? In the report of the department at page 121 reference is made to the fact that early in 1958 such a meeting was held with provincial ministers from all of the 10 provinces and at that meeting a committee was established on a continuing basis for the purpose of maintaining a continuing interest and concern in civil defence policy between the


two jurisdictions. When was the last meeting held? To what extent are the provinces fully acquainted with all of the plans of the federal government? What about the question that I have just mentioned, the ultimate authority and chain of authority? What is the situation with regard to compensation agreements? Have all the provinces now an agreement with the federal government in the matter of compensation?
I understand that in January of last year an extension was made to some of the agreements covering enrolled civil defence workers while engaged in operations arising out of natural disaster as opposed to civil defence. Since the minister deals with sirens, line rental and maintenance, as indicated in the report at page 123, what is the situation in that regard? Are sirens still regarded as effective instruments of alert? Under which minister does a matter of this kind come?
With regard to the information services division, is there a special civil defence information service division serving all the departments concerned, or is there an information service division in the matter of civil defence for each department? These are questions to which I think we should have some reply.
Then I should like to know from the minister how many civil defence workers on the health and welfare side he estimates we now have in the country? If he is in a position to give us the over-all picture that will also be of immense value.
On the welfare side, which is unmistakably, of course, the responsibility of the minister, I understand that at the end of 1959 we had some progress in the organization of welfare services in at least five provinces. These provinces I think were Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Has there been any expansion since that time?
In the field of emergency feeding, what progress has been made in developing the program the government had in mind when it made its report?
Now the minister in his report at page 26 says that some time ago seven hospital disaster institutes were held across the country for the purpose of studying hospital disaster plans. When was that? Was it in 1959 or in 1958? Have there been any similar institutes held in the past year? This is obviously a matter that comes within the present responsibilities of the minister. Were there any courses held at the civil defence college within the last calendar or fiscal year for physicians, dentists and other health workers? Perhaps the minister would give us an indication of the work that is now being done by the radiological defence group. This

is a very important matter. Some reference was made to some aspects of this today in another context by the minister, but perhaps he would find it possible to expand his remarks in this connection.
Then I should like to ask the minister what progress has been made with regard to civil defence organization in the civil service itself. These are some of the matters to which I direct the minister's attention in an effort to try to assist him in what I recognize at once is a very difficult task.

Mr. Chairman, there is a matter that I wish to point out to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois), and one that I usually raise every time his estimates are being considered by the house. The minister probably knows what I have in mind. It is about the dividing line between the province of Quebec and Ontario in lake St. Francis and in one section of the St. Lawrence river.
I should like to call his attention to this problem again this year, because I think that there might be some chance of finding some answer to it.
In order to be brief and not to delay the house unduly, I shall recall only the broad lines of the problem.
The south boundary between Ontario and Quebec on the St. Lawrence river has never been marked. All other boundaries, to the east, west and north, with a small exception, have been settled as a result of acts of parliament. But the boundary dividing the provinces of Ontario and Quebec has not. This matter has been outstanding for 40 years.
5346	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys Attempts were made to settle it, boards were established by both provinces and a great deal of progress was made.
I think that this line which runs from la Pointe-au-Beaudet to the international boundary between Canada and the United States opposite Cornwall and which is perhaps 25 miles long has been marked, except for a distance of about 10 miles. It is this 10 mile boundary that should be defined by a board of some sort.
I am convinced, as I have already stated on more than one occasion, that this matter does not strictly come under federal jurisdiction. It is under federal jurisdiction indirectly, so that if both provinces could reach an agreement, the federal government could pass legislation for the purpose of marking this boundary. But the point on which I wish to call the minister's particular attention is that in several instances, I suggested to him that if he invited those two governments to set up such a board, the problem might be settled once and for all.
The circumstances are quite different today from what they were two years ago. Since the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway, there has been a channel extending more on the north side of the St. Lawrence than on the south side. Perhaps some agreement might be reached with the two provinces partly on the basis of that channel. I realize that the matter has been considered, and I know there are a few islands at the upper end of lake Saint Francis that are a cause of dispute between the two provinces. However, while those islands were tremendously important some 20 or 25 years ago-I am not saying they have no importance today-they have lost some of their importance. The federal government is interested in the problem, because it is holding those islands in trust for the Indians. I would ask the minister, therefore, when he deals with the various questions that have been put to him, to tell us whether he intends to make another attempt at settling this problem.
Oh, I am afraid the minister will give me quite a different answer now, because of the recent events.

It is a very delicate problem for people living on both sides of the boundary between Ontario and Quebec. I am speaking, more particularly, of the citizens in the riding of Huntingdon in the province of Quebec, and of the counties of Glengarry and Stormont in Ontario.
The suggestion would prove to be of benefit, not only with regard to the administration of the fishing and hunting legislation, but in the case of accidents which are always liable to happen on the seaway.
As a matter of fact, if there were some accident, if two ships collided, for instance, causing severe damage, it might very well happen that nobody would know if the civil code, which is recognized in Quebec, or the common law of Ontario would apply.
There is no need to stress the point any further. I know that the minister noted my remark, because he told me so personally.
May I only remind him, knowing how kind he is, to ask the governments concerned to establish some commission which would, once and for all, settle that delicate matter.

Mr. Chairman, the last time the estimates were before the committee the hon. member for Yukon did not have an opportunity to get on with his remarks. My speech was incomplete on the first day. The minister spoke to me afterwards about one of my remarks in which I had suggested that the Canadian metal mining association had indicated it wanted a restricted rather than an expanded research program on the part of the government. I have also been in touch with the Canadian metal mining association and I have the original clipping from which I gained the impression. I do not want to apologize particularly, but I took the wrong interpretation from the information I had. In actual fact the association was, I understand, willing to go along with the minister's suggestion that the mining research organization should handle production and ore problems, while the federal government mines department concentrated on basic

research. I should explain to the minister that my reason for pushing the interpretation further was the result of a personal conversation I had with someone in the metal mining association who did not represent the official view of the association.
One point I wanted to make to the minister is that in our part of the country there is great concern over the fact that if it is at all possible for a direct reduction steel mill to come into existence we think it would be a powerful thing for our economy. One of the minister's own economists, Mr. Elver, has made an analysis and indicated that either Port Arthur or Seven Islands would be an economic site.
One of the suggestions that has been put forward by groups in our area is that the government consider some kind of subvention such as that now offered to the maritime coal people in order to get their material into the central Canadian market. This suggestion is that a subvention or a subsidy be given in a rather revolutionary approach to get this direct reduction mill into operation. This is something that is completely new in North America, this kind of mill is rather revolutionary and I believe the idea of a subsidy would be revolutionary, too. Perhaps the economist who made this estimation of the prospects for the iron ore industry in Canada might consider what a policy of subventions of various kinds, such as developmental rates, might do for progress in this field.
I feel there will be an important contest in the next decade between Canadian iron ore resources and Venezuelan and African resources in competing for a share of the United States and European markets. Any assistance that we could get that would enable us to get a producer into the field now, especially with such a high value product as is put out by a direct reduction mill, would be of great value.
The last point I want to make concerns, in a sense, an apology to the house. A number of weeks ago I brought up a question with the Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with the uranium industry and the tremendous number of telegrams that had been received by the hon. member for Assiniboia as well as other members of the house. I understand the telegrams numbered well over 2,000, and they were dispatched to Ottawa in order to sway political opinion here in favour of Rio Tinto's plans to amalgamate or take up some of the contracts that existed. I think the minister and hon. members may be interested in knowing that the hon. member for Assiniboia and I took the trouble to send replies to several hundred of these people.

The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is of great importance to the people of my riding, and I hope any remarks I make this evening will indicate just how important I think the department is in so far as the development of the rest
5348	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys of the nation is concerned. I feel that nothing is more basic or more fundamental, nothing is more vital to the advance of Canadian human and material betterment, than the work of this department.
One thing stands out most clearly from the evidence heard while the estimates of this department were before the standing committee on mines, forests and waters last year, that is, the failure of government for at least 10 and, in some branches 25 years to recognize the value of the work of the department. Not only has there been a continuous disregard of the material benefits to Canada which would have resulted from allowing the department to fully perform its proper function but the skill and brilliance of the departmental scientific and technical personnel has gone almost unnoticed, and their counsel and advice unheeded. Over many years, at least a decade, there have been clear and persistent indications of the need for reform. For just as long and just as clear have been the indications of the important benefits to Canada which would be the natural and inevitable result flowing from these reforms. But the need and the importance of the need were either ignored or neglected year after year.
The kindest thing that can be said for the Liberal administration in this regard is that they failed to realize the real significance of the work being produced by the department, that they remained for so many years in ignorance of the true value of this work and its relation to all phases of Canadian development. If they did realize the significance of the contribution to be made by the work of the department, their failure to do anything about it amounts to the grossest neglect of their duty while in office.
I submit that the evidence given before the standing committee last session stands as a massive indictment against the former administration to which they may plead either ignorance or neglect but to which they cannot be heard to plead innocence.
I have said that there is no single phase of the economic life of this nation that is not affected by the work of this department. Despite this very important fact, however, the restrictions which have been placed upon the functions of the department in past years have relegated it to playing an insignificant role in national development. When it had so much to offer, advantage was not taken of its capacities. It became the orphan of government and continued to be regarded as such over the years.
This is the condition then that faced this government when it first took office in June of 1957. Members know that one of the first


steps taken by this government during the first session of parliament after the present cabinet took office was to reactivate the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, a committee which had lain dormant for over 22 years during Liberal administration. In my opinion the first fruits of the work of this committee have been realized. The searching inquiry conducted into the function of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has resulted in the production of a useful report to the house.
It would be exceedingly difficult to exaggerate the importance of the functions of this department. Its chief role should be regarded, I feel, in the light of the significance of the Canadian mineral industry. The significance of minerals in providing the material basis for the economic life and social organization of humanity has long been recognized. Our civilization today, more than ever before, depends for its continuance on the minerals which permit and sustain its existence. The geometric increase and the concentration of world populations, the frequency and speed of movement of transport, the extent and quality of human control over the forces of nature are all directly dependent upon the discovery and utilization of mineral resources. It is, therefore, of prime importance that we in Canada should have as accurate information as can be obtained about the extent of the available reserves in this field.
It would be a great mistake to assess the functions and the needs of this department on the basis only of the requirements today. And it is not enough to simply say "We will not make such a mistake" without giving a good deal of thought to the reasons for saying such a thing. I believe there are sufficient indications of the trend of future demands for minerals as to warrant the assertion that Canada must be prepared to meet the needs of 10, 20 or 30 years from now. Indeed, there is no reason why we should not, in our considerations, contemplate the fact that upon the expiration of a century from now all world sources of minerals will likely have been exhausted. There are a number of very basic factors which justify taking this position. I feel that these factors are clearly distinguishable now, but before discussing them I should like for a moment more to deal with the importance of minerals to Canadians today and tomorrow, all in the light of the objectives which should be those being pursued by this department. A good many of the department's requirements and shortcomings are known now, thanks largely to the examination of departmental activities and deficiencies by the mines, forests and waters committee last session.

It is very difficult to chart future courses but I think all will hasten to agree that we must make a concerted effort to do so; and in doing so I do not think it would be desirable for us to confine ourselves to domestic needs and trends. In so far as the world picture is concerned, the more optimistic observers point out that there is today no serious or general shortage of any essential metallic or non-metallic mineral product. These people say that the discovery of new sources has always kept abreast of the increasing demand and, further, that new discoveries combined with increased efficiency in methods of processing and utilization will be adequate to meet any future needs.
How about the pessimists? They emphasize, and rightly so, the fact that mineral resources are wasting assets. They are not replaceable as are our agricultural products, our forest products and the like. Once the mineral content supplied by nature in the crust of the earth has been exhausted either by wasteful or beneficial use, it cannot be restored. These people say that the rate of consumption today presents an entirely new problem for which past experience gives no assurance of a solution.
But there is one thing that all scientists agree on and that is the necessity of maintaining an ample supply of minerals and metals if our civilization, as we know it, is to be maintained or if further progress is to be made. Iron, copper, lead, zinc, nickel, aluminum, magnesium and other base metals are, by definition fundamental to our way of life. Almost equally important are such alloying metals as manganese, chromium, molybdenum and tungsten, which are essential to the steel industry. The industrial minerals, limestone sulphur, salt and fluorspar supply the raw materials for much of the world's chemical industry, while the mineral fertilizers, phosphate rock and potash, are of growing importance in agriculture. Without these or effective substitutes large segments of the prospective population of the earth will be condemned to lives of misery and degradation.
Eminent scientists have said that the implications of these facts raise a problem so vast and of such universal incidence that in a sane world they would be made the immediate subject of common study and cooperative planning. The best proof of this statement is to be found in the difficulties that are being experienced in adapting atomic energy to beneficial rather than to destructive uses. In the race between education and catastrophe, education is falling farther and farther behind.
Business of the House
I said earlier that we are justified in stating that within the century ahead we can see the exhaustion of practically all known ore deposits and that there were a number of factors that justified such an assertion. The first of these is the rapidity with which the number of human beings on the earth is increasing. This geometric increase is resulting in the addition of some 122,400 births every day or 45 million per year. In the 30 minutes allowed me to speak here 2,550 more humans are born than have died.
A second fundamental factor is the almost universal demand for a higher standard of living. This will mean, inevitably, an expansion of the demand for mineral products. In fact, it is quite clear that the combination of an increasing population and rising standards of living will place a strain on world metal resources which will almost certainly in the end prove beyond the capacity of man and nature to supply.
I do not think I need dwell at any length upon the importance of these factors in the common western fight against the spread of communism.
May I now say a brief word on conservation. I think it is important to observe that since 1914 the depletion of world mineral resources has been proceeding at an unexampled rate. It should cause us all to pause for serious reflection to realize that the quantity of mineral products consumed between 1914 and 1949-that is 35 years-far exceeds that of the whole preceding period of man's existence on earth. It is a fearful realization that human intelligence has allowed a great proportion of the minerals used in the last 50 years to be criminally wasted in the most destructive wars in history.
As world resources of metals are exhausted the significance of Canada as a major supplier increases. The importance of the work of this department becomes even more significant as we consider the factors affecting resource consumption.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):

subtopic: EUROPEAN COMMON MARKET
subsubtopic: IMPOSITION OF AGRICULTURAL IMPORT CONTROLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem of what may happen within the common market concerning its agricultural policy has been under study now for several years. I spoke on this subject at the GATT conference in 1957, and ever since then at the ministerial level and through official channels we have expressed our point of view concerning the agricultural policies which might be developed by the Six.
At the present time the representatives of Canada, the United States, Australia, New Zealand and Argentina are participating in a round of informal consultations with the common market countries regarding the agricultural policies of the European economic community. The Canadian delegation is headed by Mr. J. H. Warren, assistant deputy minister of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Representatives of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Finance are included in the delegation. That delegation will, in the course of consultation with representatives of the common market, once again express the point of view of Canada and urge that restrictions be not placed against our trade in agricultural products.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It is my intention, Mr. Chairman, to speak for only a few minutes, having had the pleasure of acting as chairman of the committee to which the minister made some detailed reference. May I therefore, at the outset, join with many hon. members of the house who have congratulated the minister on the manner in which he has conducted the affairs of his department during the past year; and in particular may I thank him on behalf of the committee for the great co-operation which he and his departmental officials extended to us during several weeks of intensified hearings.
First of all I should like to say that I recognize that I have no authority to make these comments as chairman of the committee and that these remarks are not intended in any way to serve as a rebuttal to the statement of the minister. However, having had the responsibility of compiling the report I thought I would make one or two references to the statement, perhaps by way of explanation or clarification of the references contained in the report of the estimates committee. In so doing, while the minister has already indicated the great degree of unanimity in the views of the committee and his departmental officials, I hope I can illustrate that we are even closer together in our views than his statement might have indicated at first glance.
Supply-Health and Welfare
In his opening remarks the minister made reference to our conclusions with respect to the hospital bed shortage in Canada. If I may quote from his statement as found at page 5246 of Hansard, he said in part:
I can assure the committee that the department is also concerned with this matter. At the same time we have serious doubts as to whether the suggested immediate review on a nation-wide basis of the availability of beds in relation to demand would be the most effective approach.
He then went on to point out the responsibility in the first instance of the provinces in dealing with this matter, with which, of course, the committee agrees. The explanation that I would make to him and to his department officials is just this. Throughout the entire report we were very conscious of the thin line separating the responsibility of the federal government and that of the provinces. We realized that in many of our recommendations we were indeed treading on dangerous ground having regard to the impropriety of making recommendations affecting the responsibility of the provinces. But having said that, we should also state that we felt that even though the responsibility in the first instance lies with the provincial authority, this fact does not relieve the federal government from some responsibility as well. If I may, I should just like to make reference to the recommendation itself with regard to the hospital bed shortage in Canada:
.. . the committee recommends that the relationship between the three levels of government be examined-first, to determine the seriousness of the hospital bed shortage in Canada by instituting an immediate review of availability in relation to demand;
Second, by discussing the results of this survey with provincial and municipal authorities so that any future critical bed shortage may be averted;
Third, in co-operation with the provinces, by attacking the problem of chronic bed care, with a view to providing increased accommodations for the more critically ill patients.
In all three references we acknowledge the responsibility of the provinces. We also accept the view of the minister that every effort should be made by the provinces to determine what is their problem with respect to the hospital bed shortage. However, it seems important to us, if only to standardize the review in order to determine what is the seriousness of the problem, that this could best be initiated by the federal authority. This does not, Mr. Chairman, in any way offend the rights of the provinces. It merely assists them, and of course the federal government, in coming to some conclusion on the question of how we can resolve this serious problem.
I would point out that there is not a city in Canada that is not concerned with the problem. That being the case, we concluded that the federal government as such could do

Supply-Health and Welfare a service to the provincial and municipal authorities by assisting in a review to ascertain how great the problem actually is.
The next point to which the minister took some exception dealt with the question of closed hospitals. In fact he said that his most serious exception to our recommendation was what he described as a basic disagreement with the implication of the committee's comment relating to this problem. I do not intend to argue the point at all, but merely point out that in the final paragraph of his statement dealing with this problem he said this, as reported at page 5247 of Hansard:
While I cannot therefore agree with such an action-
The action of the committee, or the recommendation of the committee.
-I would emphasize that the department does have a definite interest in this matter, and we have expressed this interest through what we consider to be the proper channels-
From this I think it is right to conclude that the committee had brought to the attention of the minister the problem of which he has been well aware, and that we disagree only on the method by which this problem should be approached, not on the existence of the problem.
There are a number of other items on which the committee and the department, through the minister, have expressed general agreement. The item with respect to civil defence and the emergency measures organization perhaps is one obvious example. The minister rightly points out that some of the recommendations of the committee are outside the jurisdiction or the authority of his department, and that he has referred those recommendations to the departments that are concerned with them.
He then went on to point out the progress that has been made on health studies with respect to his own department. We of the committee, of course, were happy to learn of this progress and I congratulate him on it, but perhaps the one point I would make is this. He discussed the amount of literature or pamphlets which are currently being printed or are under review. I would ask permission to draw to his attention the one reference we made in this respect, and which reads as follows:
(d) Information in either pamphlet form or through visual aids should be reassessed so that in the event of a national emergency, instructions will be expressed in concise and simple terms, thus avoiding confusion by too many complicated orders.
In other words the committee, or at least this member of the committee, expressed the view that the essential thing is to have the

population realize, in the event of an emergency, what action they must take immediately. We must avoid any risk or any danger of overcomplicating the problem by overwhelming our people with too much information or too many pamphlets.
The next reference which the minister made deals with the comment in our report concerning the difficult problem of publications within his department. He pointed out that these publications have provided a very useful service, and in that the committee concurs. He went on to state that provincial authorities have, in the first instance, requested these publications, and of course, this is true. I would point out however that when the cost is so small to the province it is perhaps understandable that these publications would be requested in great volume. We also acknowledge, sir, that in many instances these publications have been extremely useful, and it would undoubtedly cause some distress if they were all eliminated.
What we do ask, though, is whether the department should' not review an item which represents something in the vicinity of $400,000 to the government and which involves a staff of 33 people, to ascertain whether, in relation to the cost, the department and the country are receiving fair value for this expenditure. I feel this is a sound argument. The minister agreed, as the report points out, that this comes under the heading of information. Here again I am happy to note that the minister intends to keep this matter constantly under review.
In his reference to the efficiency evaluation of the department the minister rightly took credit for the fact that the committee were not able to find any breakdown in operational efficiency of the department. He then went on to make reference, as the committee did in its report, to the number of surveys and reviews which have been made by the methods division of the civil service commission. Our whole approach in making our recommendations assumed that further reviews would be made by this organization. We have looked at the type of surveys that have been made by the methods division in the past, and in each instance, taking a particular segment of the department, there is no evidence to suggest that this is in any way related from one department or one division of the department to another.
We suggest, therefore, and I think rightly so, a survey of a nature which would make an over-all estimation of such problems as overlapping of responsibility. Such a survey would no doubt be useful. We need not remind the committee, Mr. Chairman, that the department under review is one of the largest in terms of the expenditure of money,

spending something over a billion dollars. This need not be construed as meaning that the department is necessarily not inefficient, but quite the reverse. It means that if it is to maintain its present status these reviews from time to time could maintain its operational efficiency and therefore would be extremely useful to the minister. Here again I am happy, Mr. Chairman, that the minister concurs when he suggests that he has some sympathy for this recommendation as well.
I finally come, sir, to the one reference I would make outside of the minister's report in which he lumped together a number of recommendations and categorized them as part of government policy. Of course the committee recognizes them as such. There is one in particular however, the blind pension, payable to our handicapped in Canada to which I should like to refer.
We argue, sir, that not just from a humanitarian point of view but also from a basis of a practical policy our recommendation to eliminate the means test makes good sense and has validity. If this action were taken, this group of people who suffer such an unusual handicap would be encouraged to rehabilitate themselves to a greater degree and thus conceivably make of themselves even more useful citizens. We hope, therefore, that the government, the minister and his colleagues, will give special consideration to this recommendation.
I do not propose to go on, sir. I wanted to make reference only to those items, as I said, by way of explanation and not by way of disagreement. Perhaps it is significant to note, Mr. Chairman, that this department was under review by the committee during some 18 meetings, and on examination of its activities has produced what we hope will prove to be constructive suggestions rather than anything in the nature of serious criticism of the functions or operations of this department. As a private member of that committee I would be one of the first to congratulate the minister and his officials.
On this note, sir, I shall resume my seat and thank the minister again for his reference to the committee's work. We sincerely trust that in the not too distant future he and his officials will again come before the estimates committee.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, rarely do I speak at such length that my remarks have to be continued in the next edition of Hansard. However, I am interested in this question, and I do wish to complete bringing to the attention of the committee the recommendations contained in the policy statement of the Canadian welfare council. Last evening when I was required to take my seat
Supply-Health and Welfare because my 30 minutes had expired, coincidental with the arrival of six o'clock, I had dealt with all the recommendations up to No. 16. I now wish to continue the recommendations. I quote:
17.	The dominion government should create in the Department of National Health and Welfare consultative and technical services in welfare, analogous to those now available in health. These services should include such technical advice as may be required in, for example, statistical reporting, and the professional consultation that may be useful in such matters as the care of the aged, problems of social welfare administration and staff training.
18.	The dominion government should contribute substantially to the cost of professional and in-service training required in the administration of social security programs.
I think that is a very good suggestion indeed.
19.	The dominion government should make funds available for demonstration and research projects, in the causes and prevention of dependency, social and economic rehabilitation, and similar problems.
We see the need for that to an increasing extent in the various communities in Canada.
20.	Machinery should be devised to ensure regular communication among provinces, and between provinces and the dominion government, on all welfare matters of common interest.
I might say at this stage that I am very pleased to note that they always refer to the federal government as the "dominion" government.
21.	The dominion government should establish a broadly representative body of competent persons, the purpose of which would be to keep under constant review all aspects of Canada's social security program and to advise on changes and improvements that may from time to time be desirable.
I think that really does provide for cooperation and an exchange of competent persons across the country in a continuing review of the changing circumstances, the changing needs, and the need for changed programs to meet those needs.
Then the final recommendation, No. 22, reads as follows, and I am very interested in this one:
22.	The dominion government should appoint a royal commission to study all aspects of social security for which it has a direct or indirect responsibility and more particularly to make recommendations with respect to:
a.	Gaps in existing provisions and priorities in dealing with unmet needs.
b.	The appropriate methods of providing social security benefits, whether by social insurance, statutory social welfare payments, public assistance, or by a combination of these methods, in respect of old age, unemployment, sickness, disability, death of the breadwinner and the cost of child rearing.
c.	The development of a more integrated system of social security.
d.	Federal-provincial co-operation in the field of social security.
5292	MOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare
e.	The negotiation of reciprocal agreements with other countries in order to provide social security coverage on an equitable basis for immigrants to Canada and for Canadians residing in other countries.
f.	Other questions having to do with the design, content and administration of Canada's total social security system.
The council suggests that in the selection of members of the royal commission account should be taken of cultural differences, and of the need to include people with practical and theoretical knowledge of social welfare and social security.
I think the final paragraph is well worth reading into the record:
The appointment of a royal commission would ensure that these problems receive the thoughtful consideration they require. It would also provide an opportunity for interested and informed groups to appear and present their views. Only through such careful study and wide consultation can we be certain that the kind of design and structure toward which we move in our social security system will satisfy both the needs and wishes of the Canadian people and take full account of the realities of Canadian life.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am sure all hon. members of this house receive correspondence almost daily which indicates the need for an over-all social security system. I have received a letter just this morning from a lady in my constituency whose husband has been unemployed for six months, who has done his best to obtain employment and who has exhausted his unemployment insurance benefits. The provincial authorities refuse to place him on social assistance, and he is left stranded without any source of income or any money even to travel around and try to locate employment. That type of situation arises because of the lack of an over-all social security system which dovetails the policies of the federal and provincial governments.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, let me say that I think all of us recognize this need and that it is obvious, but the need requires immediate attention. Without doubt we have the financial capacity to meet the cost of an over-all social security system. We have the administrative staff and the medical personnel. We have the technical and other staff both in the federal and provincial governments as well as in other institutions; competent, talented people capable of administering such a program. We do not go into this in darkness, because we have the experience, although the circumstances are somewhat different, of Great Britain and other western European countries to guide us. We also have the information as to the attempts in this direction in the United States; and best of all in Canada we have the experience of that


pioneering province in social security, Saskatchewan, which has now received a mandate from the people of Saskatchewan to institute a provincial health insurance scheme. No doubt within a few months we will have valuable experience as a result of the institution of that scheme.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that in the immediate future this government should attend to the urgent needs of the people, particularly with regard to old age security, old age assistance and other forms of relief which require attention, by means of amendments to social security legislation. At the same time the government should accept this recommendation of the Canadian welfare council for the appointment of a royal commission which would have the opportunity to do the things mentioned in their policy statement; which would get the views of provincial governments, municipal organizations and other organizations and interested people across Canada, and which would have not vague terms of reference but terms of reference that would authorize the royal commission to make recommendations for an over-all social security plan to meet the needs: of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, the standing committee on estimates, of which I have the honour to be a member, convened for a few days to look over all sections of the important Department of National Health and Welfare. First of all, I must say that our task was greatly facilitated by the full co-operation of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) and all the department's officials. As a matter of fact, the minister, after stating that he was very happy to take part in the discussion of his department's affairs by the members of. our committee, supplied a detailed report; which enabled us to have a good general': idea of the work to be accomplished.
According to the minister, the total estimates of his department for the year 1,9601961 would amount to $1,439,240,729, which; means an increase of more than $38 million, over those of the previous year. One-reason, for that increase can largely be attributed: to payments intended under the unemploy-, ment insurance scheme, in which the province of Quebec has decided to participate in , the future. At this stage, I am very happy to. point out that wise decision on,the part of the legislators in my province..

In future, many unemployed who are unable to work because of their age or physical handicaps will therefore receive assistance of which they had been deprived under the Disabled Persons Act. Indeed, under that legislation, assistance was available to only fully disabled people who had no hope of recovering.
Among the many items provided in the significant budget of $1,439,000,000 submitted for the Department of National Health and Welfare, there are three main ones which almost cover the whole amount. I referred to the sum of $599 million required for the Old Age Security Act, the sum of $508 million required to enforce the Family Allowances Act, and finally the sum of $167 million to pay the federal government's contribution under the provincial Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.
May I be allowed, as a doctor, to make a few comments on that last item.
As mentioned by the minister in his general report on the operations of his department, the implementation of a federal-provincial contributory hospital insurance program is just beginning. However, the budget had to increase more than twofold yearly, since 1958, to such an extent that the estimated budget for 1958, that is, $55 million, will reach $162 million for 1960-61.
With regard to those estimates, the province of Quebec remains the only province not included in that program. That abstention on the part of my province may have seemed unusual to the other nine. In this connection, I have heard here, several remarks, often commented upon in our newspapers, and which were all of a political character.
I myself, during the last session, referred here in the house to some remarks I personally heard from the late Mr. Duplessis on that matter. "Tell your colleagues in Ottawa", he told me, "that I am not opposed, in principle, to hospital insurance, but we have to be wise and honest. Wisdom compels us to see how the other provinces will fare in this field, and to benefit from their experience, favourable or unfavourable; honesty compels us to avoid establishing a hospital insurance plan before we have a sufficient number of beds to meet the needs. Nobody has the right, he added, to open a drugstore if he has not the necessary drugs to put on his shelves".
Consequently, the policy of building hospitals of all sizes and for special requirements has received a new impetus in the province

May I be allowed to point out, incidentally, that several large hospital construction projects are still under way this year. 1 would refer in particular to Savard Park hospital located in my constituency, so often referred to here and in the press, as an example of injustice towards Indians and Eskimos. That hospital will be the first of its kind to be placed at the disposal of family doctors who, until now, had the greatest difficulty in getting their patients admitted and treating them there in general hospitals.
