Unlike the latter, he must retain his freedom toward his patient, who after all is his employer, while the patient must remain free to choose his own physician. Unlike a civil servant, he has to work devotedly round the clock in his fight against disease and death, which are unpredictable and have no time limit.
I hope none of you will ever suffer a heart attack at two o'clock in the morning, at the very moment when the general practitioner or specialist, having become a civil servant, could refuse to get out of bed and answer your call until nine in the morning. A British doctor whom I met in Geneva told me he had had to wait three weeks for his turn to get a tooth pulled by the civil servant dentist, who inevitably closed his office at 5 p.m. and reopened only at 9 a.m. That just shows the drop in professional standards under state medicine. And what about a doctor's ambition to improve himself, to study and to devote himself, when he knows that his statute as a civil servant will be based less on his efficiency in treating the sick, than on his readiness to fill departmental forms. Doctors have not deserved to be drafted.
There are practically no citizens in the world except doctors who can claim to devote 18 to 20 hours a day of their time to their fellow men, and at a rate of remuneration reduced to 60 per cent in the case of the poor. The charges of greed recently levelled by a provincial premier at the doctors of his province were therefore baseless, and were just intended to justify his state medicine scheme. Under such legislation, doctors will become slaves to the state and the sick.
I therefore solemnly urge my colleagues in the noble medical profession never to lend themselves to the schemes of politicians of any colour or stripe. They will use every device they can think of to get their program through


at the expense of the medical profession, and at the expense of something we deeply cherish, the nobility of our mission, with all the freedom of action it involves.
I am pleased to mention here the position taken by the Canadian medical association, particularly by its Quebec section, at its last meeting a month ago. It passed a resolution in support of hospital insurance, but came out squarely against state health insurance. It will therefore support every form of free, noncompulsory health insurance, to which governments may perhaps contribute in favour of the poor and of the small wage earner, but it will never be persuaded to accept compulsory state insurance. It will not prostitute that noble profession, nor betray its ideals for political ends.
Then too, doctors should remain free, and their devotion should never be drafted, mainly to gratify the ambitions of politicians or socialist extremists.
I therefore urge the government never to agree to share in the costs of a policy of drafting the members of the medical profession into a state-run plan whose standards will certainly be lower.
Mr. Chairman, a third item of the estimate, which it is also very important to point out, is the one dealing with preventive medicine and general health grants. The amount included in the estimates in this regard, for 1960-61, is $63,591,941. This shows the vital role of preventive medicine and of measures to preserve our health and to prolong human life.
A learned physician and physiologist stated recently that man is built to live a hundred years or more. Hardly 30 years ago the average life expectancy was 40 years, but today it is between 68 and 70. We are therefore well on the way towards the objective suggested by our learned physiologists.
Before concluding, I want to add a few words about the very noble and honourable mission that our government entrusted to me in May 1959, when I was appointed as an observer at the 12th annual meeting of the World Health Organization in Geneva. Perhaps I should have reported immediately upon my return, but the session was drawing to a close and I have had no other opportunity until now.
I owe this honour especially to the minister of health and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker) and I take this opportunity to thank them publicly and cordially.

Our delegation was headed by Dr. G. D. W. Cameron, deputy minister of national health, a man of prestige and wide experience. Deputy head of the delegation was Mr. Wer-shop, ambassador and permanent representative at the European bureau of the United Nations.
As acting delegates we had such distinguished men as Dr. C. F. Amyot, deputy minister of health for British Columbia, Dr.
D.	B. Layton and Dr. Percy Moore, both senior officials of the department of national health, and Mr. R. X. Jay, first permanent secretary at the European bureau of the United Nations. I was therefore happy, Mr. Chairman, to be appointed as an observer with such a team, in so important a delegation.
Mr. Chairman, may I summarize now some of my impressions. This organization, a United Nations agency, is in my opinion, one of its most important ones. Because of its objective, the health and welfare of men all over the world, it is indeed the best peace organization, the most beneficent and humane one, without which peace cannot be achieved.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, during all those meetings there were no bitter discussions, none of those intractable obstinacies which, unfortunately, so often mar meetings at United Nations headquarters.
At the opening sitting, after the roll-call and the examination of delegates' credentials, Sir John Charles, chief medical officer of the department of health in Great Britain was elected chairman for the term 1959-60. Delegates from 87 regular member countries and from three associate member countries were in attendance. It was therefore a large gathering. Some representations were made by representatives of the communist bloc against the barring of continental China from a regular membership in the World Health Organization; but there were no attempts at sabotage. I might add that representatives from communist countries missed no opportunity for propaganda whenever the occasion offered.
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the barring of communist China, I daresay, speaking as a physician of course, that I found that discussion rather saddening. Indeed, when you consider the World Health Organization on a strictly medical and humanitarian basis, something comparable to the international Red Cross, it is distasteful to a doctor to think that 600 million human beings in com-79951-0-334
Supply-Health and Welfare munist China are being kept out of that essentially humanitarian organization, prevented from sharing in its great advantages, and of making their own scientific and material contributions to it.
On the other hand, if you look upon the World Health Organization as a United Nations agency, there was obviously no point in discussing the problem, at least until such time as communist China is admitted into the United Nations family.
I said a moment ago, that the WHO is doing highly humanitarian work which is needed throughout the world. I would even go further, Mr. Chairman and say that this indispensable work is being carried on particularly in underdeveloped countries. It is all to Canada's credit and honour, Mr. Chairman, to have been one of the first countries to join the WHO in 1946. Dr. Brock Chisholm, then Canadian deputy minister of health, was its first director general. It is therefore obvious that, since the start, our country has joined with the great powers in financing and promoting the establishment and growth of that peaceful organization. Its procedure is similar to that of a parliament. There is, first of all, a general meeting of all delegates to discuss the program of the session and to form committees on the various matters to be discussed; committees on health problems, on financial and legal administration, on research, on resolutions, the committee on estimates, et cetera.
The general assembly meets when necessary and is supplied with the reports of the various committees, to discuss and pass them.
Mr. Chairman, those committees discussed many of these matters, particularly the main causes of the appalling death rate in underdeveloped countries and ways to reduce it. Among the leading causes of heavy mortality are such infectious diseases as malaria, typhoid fever, smallpox, tuberculosis, leprosy and venereal diseases. However the problem of drinking water transcends all others. Water, almost to the same degree as air, is necessary to life.
My deskmate at the meeting, a delegate physician from Pakistan, stated that the average life expectancy in his country is 28 years and that 50 per cent of deaths were due to the lack of drinkable water. The water problem became the general theme because of the great number of countries which were deeply affected and interested by it.

Supply-Health and Welfare
A delegate from France even suggested that WHO should concentrate solely on the study and solution of this single problem, that of polluted water-which incidentally would have helped solve many other health problems, instead of trying to tackle all problems at once, because, he said, quoting an old French proverb:	"Grasp all, lose
all". In other words, he who tries to solve everything at once solves nothing.
Therefore, before Mr. Khrushchev offers to settle the water problem, there is urgent need for all the favoured nations in the world to take the necessary steps, at least, to supply good drinking water to the hundreds of millions of human beings who are dying of hunger, thirst and infectious diseases in underdeveloped countries. Is it believable that two persons out of three in the world do not have enough to eat, nor enough to drink, except infected water?
Very serious studies have been undertaken about the steps to be taken to control contagious diseases which are so widespread and dangerous among tropical peoples. But money will always remain the sinews of war.
The assembly expressed regret that its budget was inadequate to achieve its dedicated program of controlling malaria. To obtain additional funds it called upon governments, industries and all private organizations that are in a position to contribute towards the control of that plague, malaria, and to press further, if possible, the implementation of a health program throughout the world.
Reference was made also to special funds designed to organize research and to direct it along the efforts being made by the organization to raise health and welfare standards throughout the world. The sum of $500,000 was therefore added to the budget for research purposes.
The assembly also decided to have the necessary plans prepared for the construction of a special headquarters building for the permanent staff, and for carrying on of all the activities of the World Health Organization. The space it has occupied until now at United Nations headquarters has become inadequate. The federal government of Switzerland, and of the canton of Geneva in particular, have offered the land and their assistance in preparing the financial operation, totalling close to $7 million, involved in that construction.
Before closing its session, the World Health Organization approved a budget of $16,918,700

for the implementation of the 1960 program, Canada's contribution being fixed at $483,000.
In conclusion, I may state as an observer that it is altogether impossible to evaluate the work carried out by the World Health Organization. This work is absolutely necessary and essentially humanitarian, as I said earlier, since its purpose is the health and welfare of human beings. It is a work likely to bring peace because its object is to fight thirst, hunger, disease and death. World peace is unattainable in the presence of extreme poverty. So far, peace secured by armaments has always proved a failure. Physical and moral misery has always been the spark that ignites war.
You may be sure that our annual contribution of $500,000 to the World Health Organization fund is an investment much more likely to bring peace than the hundreds of millions of dollars that we spend each year on armaments whose effectiveness in establishing peace is not only often questionable but actually nil.

Mr. Chairman, before commencing my remarks I wish to express appreciation of the excellent address given by the hon. member for Quebec West. Those who have known him over the last number of years realize that he is one of the men most devoted to the principles of the medical profession of which he is so distinguished a member.
Having paid my respects to the hon. member, I wish now to comment on what he said. Among other things he seemed to be apprehensive about what is happening to prepaid medical care plans. This group has always advocated prepaid medical care for the Canadian people, but I believe I can honestly say that none of us has ever advocated state medicine. If we decide on how we are to pay for medical care, while at the same time leaving to the doctors the pursuance of their profession as they deem wise and advisable, we feel that is far removed from what is commonly understood to be state medicine.
I do not think our group has ever been an advocate of state medicine. All we advocate is that when we are well we pay for the days when we shall be ill, and that we all hold one another's hands so that all of us can receive the finest care that the medical profession has to offer, regardless of the financial ability of the particular individual at that time.

The hon. member may wish to make a distinction between voluntary prepaid medical care plans and prepaid medical plans operated by various levels of government. I believe that is a minor detail. Our main contention is that it is only when it comes to the matter of payment that we ought to co-operate one with another so that no one shall go without necessary medical care. I believe that in the long run it will even be of assistance to those engaged in the medical profession; because I cannot understand how a doctor, having to worry about income, can more ably attend to his work as a doctor, namely the healing of the ill, than if he does not have to worry about who is to pay the bill.
At this time I wish to express my appreciation to the minister for the courtesy and kindness that have been extended to me and, I have noted, also to other members in the opposition within the past year. I believe that all of us in this house, regardless of where we sit, are vitally interested in the work being done by the Department of National Health and Welfare. I believe the health of our people ought to supersede political interests at all times. Never, to my notice at least, has the minister replied to inquiries with a political ax hidden behind his back. He has never done that when we have asked him for information. I think that attitude is commendable.
This house is exceptional in that it contains an unusually large representation from the medical profession. However, the minister has, as had other ministers before him, made it very clear that to be vitally interested in and to have some knowledge of the work of this department and the needs of the department do not necessarily mean that one has to be a medical man. The minister has shown that an accountant can be as greatly interested in this work as can a lawyer coming out of the Windsor area.
I wish to offer a number of recommendations. My initial recommendation has to do with our whole approach to the administration of social security in this country. We have veterans pensions, family allowances, widows' allowances, mothers' allowances, pensions for the disabled, pensions for the aged, pensions for this and pensions for that, pensions for almost every other thing, each with its own administrative arrangements. I feel there is a reason for this. We have obtained what little social security we have in Canada by concessions here and concessions there, always from unwilling governments, and some have been given at election time. However, that may be a political reality or even a need in Canada.
Now that we have this vast array, this vast conglomeration of welfare and pension plans 79951-0-3341
Supply

Health and Welfare in Canada, I think the time is overripe when we should begin to think in terms of consolidation; because, as every hon. member knows, we continually meet individual Canadians who, despite our terrific array of plans designed to help the unfortunate in Canada, are left out, who do not get into any of the many existing plans and schemes. I think if we agree to broaden the base and accept the fundamental concept that no one in Canada shall have to do without the basic needs in health, education, food, clothing and housing, then we should begin a process of consolidation. I see no real, valid reason why there must be a separate plan to pay pensions to the handicapped as apart from pensions to the blind, for instance. After all, even the blind are in receipt of pensions because they are handicapped, yet we have two different administrations with all the costly overhead. And, as I said before, because of this terrifically complicated machinery, for each little new need we set up a whole new administration with its overhead; yet it fails to meet the needs of ever so many individuals as each hon. member, I am sure, has experienced.
At an early date the government might well begin an investigation in to whether it is not possible to combine most if not all of our social security measures into one social security organization. This is in existence in those countries of the world where the people did not get their social security measures by bits and pieces, where they received it all at one time. In those countries we do find this over-all administration. Here in Canada we have not arrived at our social security measures in that way; therefore we have built up organization after organization after organization without having one over-all machine adequate to meet the needs of each and every individual.
I noted what the minister had to say in regard to hospital care for those who are chronically ill. I know he has given this matter a great deal of consideration over the past year, and that some research is under way. However, I noticed the minister's great hesitation in imposing any care for chronic hospital cases upon any provincial government. I can understand why he takes that attitude, because according to the British North America Act fundamental health care is under the jurisdiction of the provinces. However, when the minister and the federal government are under attack for this lack of action in certain respects, and that attack emanates from a provincial government, then I do believe the minister would be completely within his rights if he replied to such attacks without hesitation.

Supply-Health and Welfare
What I have reference to is that at the last meeting of the British Columbia legislature the minister of health of that province explained that the reason the people of British Columbia could not enjoy chronic hospital care was that the federal government refused to make grants for the building of chronic hospitals or to pay any of the cost of the maintenance of chronic hospitals. The health minister of the province of British Columbia knows that his contention at that time was not in accordance with what the situation really is, because for many long years now Ottawa has always been ready to share on a per bed basis the cost of building hospitals designed to care for the chronically ill. I believe that right now the federal government is prepared to contribute to a program in any part of Canada for building hospitals for the chronically ill an amount of $2,000 per bed. In spite of this the minister of health in British Columbia wants to lead the people of that province to believe that Ottawa is responsible for the fact there is not any real chronic hospital care in that province.
The federal government since the introduction of the national health insurance plan has gone a little farther and, as I understand our national health insurance plan, if a province now institutes a hospital insurance plan for those within the province who need hospital care because of chronic ailments, the federal government is prepared to share, to the same extent that it shares in other hospital care matters, in the cost of such care. The federal government, therefore, by legislation is prepared to contribute toward the construction of hospitals to look after the chronically ill, and also for the maintenance of such hospitals. The British Columbia minister, I rather suspect for political purposes or in order to avoid having to face this issue as a result of the demands of British Columbia residents, unjustly attacks the federal government. I believe the federal government should immediately reply to that attack, and reply in such a manner that the residents of that province become aware of that reply.
We in British Columbia are interested in seeing that the chronically ill are given adequate hospital care at the earliest possible moment. As the minister knows quite well, our hospital insurance plan in British Columbia provides only for hospital care so long as the doctor certifies the patient as acute. Immediately the patient passes the acute stage-this applies especially to our elderly people-and the doctor declares the patient to be chronically ill, then you have to leave the hospital or pay roughly $18 a day to the hospital, or you have to go to a nursing home. If you want to enter a nursing
[Mr. Kegier.l
home the rates are $185 a month and up, and the waiting list is as long as your arm. If you have not got that amount of money you have to either impose on some relative, if you have one who is able to look after you, or you have to go to one of the many disreputable nursing homes or so-called rest homes that will accept you in exchange for your old age pension or whatever pension you get from the municipality or provincial government.
The people back home are insisting that our existing hospital insurance plan be expanded to cover those declared chronically ill. I know that the federal government, by legislation, long ago decided that if a move is made anywhere in Canada to look after the chronically ill, there will be national money available to help.
I should like to see our national health insurance plan amended to include the cost of all prescribed drugs. I believe this would, perhaps, do more than anything else to resolve the questionable prices of these commodities. I have every sympathy, Mr. Chairman, for the interests of the men engaged in the practice of medicine. In the light of the income received by a lot of other people in Canada today, I doubt whether the income of our doctors is at a level which will inspire many young men or women to spend all the necessary years in obtaining that particular degree.
However, what really upsets me is the fact that when I receive a bill from the doctor and then when I receive a bill from the druggist I very often notice that the drugs that were prescribed cost much more than the time and work of the doctor who had the responsibility of prescribing the drugs. I believe that is away out of line. The man of medicine certainly ought to receive a higher compensation than the man who mixes chemicals, who is a chemist or a scientist and who only knows how to mix up a prescription in accordance with the orders of the doctor.
I should like to plead that the government, in the light of what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and others, give serious consideration to the restoration of grants for a physical fitness program in Canada. When these grants were abolished a number of years ago that was done on the ground that few parts of Canada had taken advantage of the physical fitness legislation. I believe at that time only Saskatchewan had done so. Perhaps if the federal government again offered to share the cost of a physical fitness program, now that even such an eminent individual as the Duke of Edinburgh has made reference to the need for such a plan

in Canada, many more parts of Canada would indicate an interest and a willingness to participate.
I should like to say just a few words with regard to the physically handicapped. Mental retardation and physical handicap are often related, possibly more often than not. I note with a great deal of pleasure and satisfaction the hard work that thousands of parents in Canada are undertaking on a voluntary basis to supply education to the mentally retarded. I believe that if the federal government could aid in the cost of vocational education, and I agree that it ought to do so, then the health department ought to give some consideration as to whether in the long run it would not be more economical to help pay for the cost of providing mentally retarded children with an education. I believe that if our educational program for the mentally retarded could be greatly enhanced we might save ourselves a lot of pension money because many of these people, in later years, would not need pensions.
I should like once again to call the attention of the minister to the urgent need for establishing a portable pension plan available to all Canadians, but more specifically immediately designed for the industrial workers of Canada. I have spoken to many audiences and have asked them to indicate by a show of hands how many of them, in their lifetime, have paid into a pension fund and have later, either through some fault of theirs or through no fault of theirs, had to leave their place of employment, thus losing their pension rights. In most cases 90 per cent of those in attendance who had contributed to a plan have, somewhere along the line, lost their pension rights.
I know very well that in most cases when they leave these places of employment they can obtain a refund of their contributions. However, if most people are like me in this regard, a lump sum of money always comes in handy and may be used to buy a new car or a new television set. I do not realize that the money I am spending was really designed for my old age.
I do not think the refunds should be allowed quite so freely. I am glad that the annuities branch of the Department of Labour does not permit a refund. If you pay money into the annuities branch in order to buy yourself an annuity, that money must remain there for that specific purpose. However, because of the vagaries of the Canadian economic picture-partly, I think, because we are a growing nation-we find that less than 10 per cent of the people who today pay into a pension plan will ever receive the benefits
Supply

Health and Welfare of that pension as those benefits were designed to be paid at the time they were making their monthly payments.
I think the government could help the Canadian people to help themselves if they showed some initiative in this regard. I know there is a great deal that organized labour and employers could do. If they all invested their pension funds in the Canadian government annuities branch, our problem would automatically resolve itself. I deplore the lack of initiative on the part of labour unions and on the part of employers, when they sit across the bargaining table, in that they do not explore ways and means whereby the pension arrangements they are making with their workers shall carry the provision that the pension being arranged for will be portable and that the worker will be able to carry his pension rights with him wherever he goes, exactly as today he carries his unemployment insurance book and unemployment rights with him in moving from one employer to another or from one part of Canada to another.
I should also like to plead with the government to reconsider the level of grants it pays in the field of research in health matters. We have the heart foundation collection, the tuberculosis collection, and the diseases of children collection. We have umpteen health organizations all depending on charitable donations for their research work which is most essential. I have every respect for the voluntary efforts of tens of thousands of Canadians, and especially those of Canadian women who undertake this important and often thankless task of going out in the rain from house to house, knocking on doors and asking for donations in these multitudinous appeals. The work is necessary because there is no other way at the present time. The grants from the government are modest indeed. However, when this research turns up some useful knowledge it is added to the general pool of knowledge and everyone in Canada receives the benefit.
There is no one in this chamber who does not know that he may some day receive the benefits of the research going on with regard to heart ailments. I therefore submit that if we all share the benefits of this research work, we all should be made to share the costs as a community. I submit that this research work should not be handicapped by the lack of funds or by the lack of volunteers or by the unwillingness of some people to make voluntary contributions. Even if the government today absorbed all these organizations and the responsibility for them, I know that tomorrow there would be more volunteers for other worthy causes in Canada, and I think that is the way it ought to be.

Supply-Health and Welfare But once the need has been established and once the volunteer work has reached a certain stage of general public acceptance, then I think the government ought to move in and assume this responsibility on behalf of the people as a whole.
When the minister replies I should like him to tell us what exchange of research information is taking place between countries of the western world and countries behind the iron curtain. I believe the minister is well aware of the fact that in many respects in the field of research the medical profession in the Soviet union has made remarkable headway. I often wonder whether we in the western world receive some of the blessings of that research and, vice versa, whether the people behind the iron curtain receive the blessings of the research work that our medical scientists are doing. I know there is some medium of exchange through the auspices of the United Nations. I hope we can obtain a bit of information on that particular score.
I want to express in only one or two minutes my utter dismay at the issuance of this particular little book having to do with civil defence and entitled "Your Basement Fallout Shelter". I should like the civil defence department of the minister to be called the civil disaster plan. I believe it would be much more acceptable to the Canadian people, because we often face severe disaster in our communities. I think the population as a whole would be much more united if, behind any plans for community survival and for survival of the individual, the whole plan were called a civil disaster plan.
I am a little afraid that there may be interests at work who are attempting slowly to convince the people of North America that there is hope for survival in case of a nuclear war. I hope the Canadian people will maintain what I believe is their present position, namely that should we have a nuclear war there is no defence for the Canadian people. I hope there is not a move afoot gradually to convince them and to condition them into thinking that "maybe I and you will survive". I think we ought to realize that in case of nuclear war there is no defence and that we will not survive. I do not expect that I will survive, and I do not think any other Canadian has any logical reason to expect that he can survive the rigours of an all-out nuclear war. I hope this is not part of a process of conditioning the public mind. It is for that reason as well as for practical reasons, in order to get the public to really rally around this effort, that I believe the whole effort ought to be changed in name from civil defence to civil disaster.

"Derision", says the hon. member for Port Arthur; but yesterday the hon. member for Assiniboia did exactly what I have mentioned. As reported on page 5268 of Hansard he said:
The Canadian government should come forward now with a federal prepaid medical care act by which the federal government would co-operate with any provincial government prepared to embark on such a prepaid medical care program.
That of course is a clear call for federal aid for the Saskatchewan medical care plan.
The point I wish to draw to the attention of the minister, and my principal reason for rising at this time, is the serious situation in my view which has arisen because household chemicals are not properly labelled as to whether they are dangerous or poisonous. Many of them do not have described on the label antidotes which would provide for emergency treatment where children or even adults might take these kitchen chemicals by mistake. It is my opinion that something should be done about this problem.
In the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of June 13 appeared the headline "Coroner warns householders against household poisons", and the article under that headline sets forth the sad case of a two and one half year old boy who died of poisoning as the result of getting to a can of household chemical labelled "RX.15",

containing plant food. Apparently there was not an antidote on the can or any suggested course of emergency action. I am not suggesting, of course, that this child would be able to read the label, but certainly the parents might have been in a position to take action which could have saved the boy's life. In certain cases, I am advised by medical people, when children take substances like this that may be poisonous, if a finger is stuck down the throat or if they are given some mustard emulsion the poison may be regurgitated and the child saved. But in this particular instance the child unfortunately lost his life.
Mr. Chairman, I would urge that some action be taken to deal with this particular problem. I think it is necessary action for the protection of children and people in general in the home. It is not always possible to have a doctor immediately available, and often emergency action is required. Even when a doctor is available the doctor cannot be expected to have at his fingertips the antidote for every type of household chemical. The case I have described is by no means an isolated one but one which has occurred time after time in this country, and surely we should call for action to bring about a remedy to this problem.
I do not know whether this responsibility lies solely upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare or whether the Minister of Justice should be called upon to assist in providing a remedy under one of the acts for which he is responsible. But I would suggest that the Minister of National Health and Welfare might very well take this problem unto himself and discuss it with such members of the cabinet as may be necessary in order to bring about action whereby packages of household chemicals are labelled and indicate whether or not they are poisonous. Also they should have on the label the antidote and the required emergency remedial action in case the substance is taken by human beings.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to delay the deliberations of this committee for very long, and I think I can finish by a minute or two after one o'clock.
First of all I wish to commend the minister for his able administration of the department, and I want to compliment the hon. member for Quebec West for his very sound contribution to the deliberations of this committee this morning.
The reason I rise at this time is to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee a certain amount of consternation which was aroused among my constituents, as well as, I feel, many other people in the province of Ontario, when it was mooted in
Supply-Health and Welfare the press that the cost of hospital insurance in the province of Ontario would be increased by 10 per cent. Ontario residents are not unaware that prior to the commencement of hospital insurance, hospital rates were increased considerably. I am not prepared to say the percentage, but there was quite a considerable increase percentagewise. The residents of Ontario were sold the hospital insurance plan simply because the cost of hospitalization was getting to the point where many citizens of the province felt that unless they had a hospital insurance plan of some kind they certainly could not afford hospitalization.
So I rise to protect an increase in hospital insurance rates, and I do so also because we were told that this was going to be an economical method for the people to obtain insurance. We hear a good deal today from certain quarters about monopolies; there is a lot of complaint about monopolies on the part of companies. But the worst monoply in my estimation is a state monopoly, something against which you cannot legislate, something against which you cannot argue. It is a bureaucratic monopoly, and that I am certainly against.
If hospital rates could be increased by 10 per cent after one year without any protest from the people paying the rates, what is to hinder them being increased another 10 per cent two or three years hence? This leads to sloppy administration on the part of hospitals, and I do not think we want that.
I want to commend the hon. member for Quebec West for his plea that we evade at all possible cost what is spoken of as state medicine. I believe it is quite possible for the medical profession-and I am certain they are engaged in doing so-to work out a prepaid plan that will be acceptable to all Canadians. Then the medical profession can go on with their very worth-while work and the ill can have the doctor of their choice. Bureaucracy in the treatment of the ill is something which I personally have no wish to see.
Mention was made of annuity plans and the possibility of being able to transfer from one job to another or from one industry to another the pension plan that was commenced at an earlier date. All these pension plans are commendable, but let us look back 20 years and see what has actually happened. We must examine the value of the dollars people contributed to pension plans some years ago, and recognize that it bears no resemblance to the 50-cent pieces they draw out today. That is what inflation does. If we are going to witness a continuation of the galloping inflation that has gone on since 1945 we will witness

Supply-Health and Welfare a corresponding decline in the incentive for people to save and the ultimate destruction of all incentive so to do.
I thank the committee for its indulgence.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to make only a few brief comments this afternoon, because the field has been fairly fully covered. One comment I will make is that we are going to have more and more hospitalization costs in the future as an increasing number of our population will be people over the age of 65. In the light of medical statistics it is interesting to glance around this chamber and realize that 30 out of every 100 people in this or any other group in the country owe their lives to the miracle drugs and serums and vaccines that have been developed in the last 50 years. I have only to list a few of the significant discoveries in this field to illustrate my point.
In the early 1900's, I believe in 1906, diphtheria antitoxin was developed. This was followed by the development of typhoid fever vaccine. It is important to remember that during the time of the Boer war more people lost their lives as a result of this dread disease than lost their lives in active service. It is significant to remember, too, that the war of 1914-18 could not have been fought on the scale it was if typhoid vaccine had not been discovered.
Coming to the twenties we find that on this continent, in the city of Toronto, there was discovered one of the most important findings in the history of medicine, insulin. This is an injection of pancreas that has extended the lives of many people and enabled them to live a full life span. Those of us who are old enough to be able to look back to the time before the discovery of this drug well remember those afflicted with diabetes who had poor, frail bodies and enormous appetites, and who could not pass a pail of water or a pump without pausing for a drink, and will be grateful that this is a disease now under control.
In 1928 significant advances were made by Minot and Murphy, working in a laboratory in Chicago, with respect to the discovery of the anti-pernicious anaemia factor, from liver and stomach. This represented another great victory by science in the field of human welfare.
Then came the discovery of the sulfa drugs and their derivatives in 1935. May I remind


hon. gentlemen that dagenan and sulfa derivative was worked out after more than 600 attempts. Hundreds of scientists have worked diligently in laboratories in their search for the elusive materials that would cure human ills.
The forties witnessed the discovery of penicillin. I well remember the first case in which I used penicillin. A shot was required every two hours and there was much pain involved. Hon. gentlemen will know that further advances have been made with respect to this drug, and it is no longer even necessary to take penicillin through a needle. It may be taken by tablet, and only one dose is required in a 24-hour period.
I have listed a few of the advances made by science over the years. Not long after the discovery of penicillin came the discovery of the new antibiotic drugs, the myocins; achromycin, terramycin, chlormycin, ilo-tycin and other derivatives that have saved countless human lives.
My friend the hon. member for Welland in his excellent speech dealt with his experience as a general practitioner. He recalled to my mind that in the early days when we were called out by a patient with pneumonia we went with the knowledge that one out of every five persons suffering from pneumonia was doomed to certain death. Today it is possible to go to a doctor and be cured of pneumonia within a few days. This in itself is of vast economic assistance to Canadians, not only in work hours saved but in eliminating hospital costs and in the prevention of suffering.
The speed with which many illnesses can now be retarded or cured results in decreased costs for many Canadians. The advances made -by science have also served to increase longevity in the population. As an illustration, may I point out that during the last 50 years the general population of Canada has increased two and a half times but that portion of the population age 65 years and over has increased four times in that same period. I do not have to point out that this will mean that there will be an increasing number of people in hospitals.
At the turn of the century, life expectancy was under 50 years. Today a child coming into the world can look forward to 70 years of life. This, however, is creating a problem in the field of employment and in other fields. For instance, the cost of hospitalization and welfare will continue to rise at a rapid rate as more people reach advanced age.
I suggest that it is not fair to put people age 65 and over suffering from chronic diseases in general hospitals along with persons who are under active, acute treatment.

I do not think you have to stretch your imagination very much to realize that the person who is acutely ill, whose life is hanging in the balance, will probably get the major share of the treatment, and that the older person with the chronic disease will not get the aggressive treatment that he would receive, perhaps, if there were a wing put on to that hospital where all those cases of people over 65 suffering from chronic diseases could be treated in accordance with what their condition demands.
I have only to recall to the committee that in 1920 I do not think there was a pediatric unit across Canada, if my memory serves me correctly. I well remember that when I was a student a few years later a pediatric wing was organized in the Kingston General hospital under Dr. MacGregor; and to tell you that the establishment of that pediatric unit as part of the general program of establishing chairs and professorships in our universities has cut our infant mortality so that today we can boast of life expectancy of 70 years for a child born in this country today is just to remind you of the results of our work in the field of pediatrics over the years.
I should like to suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the same principles and the same practice be followed by our hospitals today in the care of the increasing number of people in the geriatric class; that the same procedure be followed with chairs set up in universities and departments headed up with people concerned with the treatment of those older people. I think we would find that hospital costs would be cut considerably and that the people in the older age brackets would get better and more efficient treatment.
I wish to dwell on this for one more minute. There has been some talk about building separate units. I do not go along with that at all simply for the reason that we have to train medical students. Those medical students will be going out as general practitioners. They need all the knowledge of the treatment of those cases they can possibly get. I would remind you further that in the care of those cases certain drugs and certain types of treatment will be used, and the general practitioner will require to know about them. If they were put in separate units the tendency would be, in my opinion, to make the teaching inadequate.
I should like to dwell for a moment or two on the matter raised by an hon. member who said that only 200 British doctors had migrated to Canada and therefore conditions must be satisfactory in the old country. I have only this to say. When a doctor graduates from a university in another land and then comes to Canada, in most of the 79951-0-335
Supply-Health and Welfare provinces he is required to write another council examination. It is pretty difficult for a fellow who has been in practice a number of years to remember all the scientific theory that he was taught. The remark was made that there were 60,000 doctors in the United Kingdom. If my memory serves me correctly there are only 50,000. I know this is just an error in figures, but I do wish to point out that the figure of 200 is no criterion of the satisfaction or dissatisfaction of the doctors in Great Britain. The fact is that it is difficult to pull up your roots, go to another country and write examinations before you can practise.
I just bring this to your attention, Mr. Chairman. In Saskatchewan, where people are inclined to say "Here comes the golden age", according to statistics one third of the doctors practising in that province are from Great Britain. I am wondering why that province has such a high percentage of British doctors when the rest of the country does not have that percentage. Maybe there is an answer to it.
I am also wondering about this. The golden age which they talk about in the province of Saskatchewan is in a little difficulty, or was in a little difficulty, with the hospitalization plan; because Dr. Erb, who I believe is their minister of health, stated that something had to be done to cut down on these spiralling costs. It was suggested to him by the head of the college of physicians and surgeons of that province that perhaps a deterrent would have to be added to control hospitalization.
I am just giving these facts, not to condemn any plan that will give the Canadian people the best of care, because I am sure every hon. member would want to do that. I hope we shall never let politics interfere with the profession or with the training schools in the United States of America and Canada, the countries that have given us the highest standards of medical practice in the world today, that have given us most of the major discoveries in the last 50 years.
When we consider some of the places that are state controlled perhaps we should hark back and take Russia, as leader of the communist world. We can state that there has not been one major discovery in medicine or one major advance in the field of medical science come out of Russia in the last 40 years. I am not saying that we should not have forms that are changed a little from what we have today; that may be necessary in a changing world.
I do wish to refer to New Zealand as an example of socialized medicine. We hear people stating over and over again that 52

Supply-Health and Welfare per cent of the doctors there practise outside the hospitals and 48 per cent practise in the hospitals, all graduates of the same schools. The 52 per cent who practise outside are the have-nots and the fellows on the inside are the haves. Their social legislation brought them to the point where they were almost bankrupt. I talked to many of the doctors, both the ins and the outs, and I wish to tell you that I did not find any of them perfectly satisfied with those plans. I had the same experience in England where I talked to some gentlemen on the inside and some on the outside whose names I will not mention. The fellows on the inside were getting better pay. You would think they would be satisfied but they said, "No, we do not believe in any system that tends to downgrade the fellow who graduates from the same school we did and from that day onward is an outside fellow, as compared with the fellow on the inside". This is the answer to those people who say that this is the system, this is heaven. It is not. I ask the committee to weigh all the facts and not just be swayed by some written arguments to the end so that any change we inaugurate in this country will be right and proper and best for all the people.
I want to spend a minute on rising medical costs. The hon. member for Middlesex West spoke about this. We have been told some of the reasons why our people are living longer. We in the field of medical science are responsible for that. I think every doctor and scientist in Canada will surely take pride in that, but I also want to recall to the attention of the committee that many of those people have given gratuitously of their services on boards or as nurses receiving small pay and working 12-hour days. When I was in hospital in those days the nurses took their 12-hour shifts. I remember the dear old superintendent we had. She supervised everything. She made up her books at night, and if anybody was short or off she covered up. She had an 18-hour day. I remember the personnel, the nurses in training. I recall back to the days when some of them just got enough to buy their stockings and their shoes. If they got more than that they were lucky. We do not want to go back to those days, and I am not suggesting that we should.
I want to pause now to pay a compliment to that great group of nursing sisters and nurses of all faiths who did such a great job in those training hospitals and are still doing it. They have made a wonderful contribution. They gave us the care that has enabled many of us to be in this house today, and the drugs that were developed through a system of


individual enterprise that stimulated freedom of thought and action to its fullest extent.
So in conclusion, I say that the cost of hospitalization has risen simply because two thirds of that cost represents the cost of labour; that is the situation. Does anybody want to cut costs by decreasing the payment to labour? Only one third of the cost is made up in other ways.
Then someone mentioned the high cost of drugs. There is one drug item I might mention which was used in this hospital that I selected at random, the cost of which represents only 4.5 per cent of the total cost of these lifesaving drugs. These drugs can save you anywhere from one week to four weeks of hospitalization in cases of pneumonia and other diseases. I remember the cases of appendicitis that we used to see in which the appendix had ruptured, and now as a result of these drugs such patients may be out in a week. These are the contributions these drugs have made to us.
There are one or two other things upon which I should like to dwell for a moment. The first is disabled persons; I noticed that someone referred to them. I want to say that in my opinion the examination policy respec-ing disabled persons by both provincial and federal governments may be wrong. I am not saying it is, but I am wondering about this policy. I recall a case in which I was interested during the time the hon. member for Essex East was minister. This was a difficult case, and this fellow was positively entitled to a pension. The pension was turned down by Ottawa. I knew the case well, and I knew it was grossly unfair to turn down the application for pension. I am wondering, therefore, whether we should perhaps take a long look at that situation and eliminate the doubling up on these examinations.
The other thing about which I want to speak is the provision of adequate shelters in our hospitals. I am wondering if this is being done. This thought occurred to me when we were talking about shelters the other day. It appears as though we are going to have to make preparations, such as the construction of shelters, for a long time to come. If that is true I am wondering whether we are looking at this problem realistically. Perhaps these shelters should be built in when hospitals are constructed, and perhaps they should even be built into houses constructed under the National Housing Act; because I am sure everyone will admit that it appears the need for them will not be removed in the foreseeable future.
The next thing about which I am wondering is our training of medical personnel. I just
